title: Constantinople III, 681
hook: Christ has a truly human will as well as a divine one

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chalcedon: one person, truly God and truly man, who wept at the tomb and called Lazarus out. Your line was two natures, one christ.

A garden at night, across the valley from Jerusalem. Jesus has gone a little apart from his friends, and Luke's Gospel says he kneels and prays: "Father, if thou wilt, remove this chalice from me: but yet not my will, but thine be done." Read it slowly. There is a will that would rather the cup pass, and there is a yes. Long afterward, bishops argued over that one sentence, because it holds a question: when Jesus says my will, whose will is that? The answer came from the council called Constantinople the Third.
screen: `A GARDEN AT NIGHT.` → `REMOVE THIS CHALICE FROM ME.` → `WHOSE WILL IS THAT?`

segments.voice: After Chalcedon said Christ has two natures, some tried a middle road to bring divided churches back together. Fine, they said, two natures, but only one will: the divine will doing all the willing, the humanity just carried along. It sounded peaceful. Others saw the cost. Gregory of Nazianzus had put the principle long before: what Christ did not take on, he did not heal. A monk remembered as Maximus the Confessor argued that a human nature without a human will isn't fully human, and tradition says he paid dearly for saying so. The Catechism gives the council's answer: at the sixth ecumenical council, Constantinople III, in 681, the Church confessed that Christ has two wills and two natural operations, divine and human. And they are not opposed. His human will does not resist his divine will; it follows it, submits to it. Go back to the garden. Not my will, but thine. As the council's defenders saw it, if Jesus had no human will, there would be nothing to surrender, and those words would be play-acting. Because he does, the garden is real: a real human wanting, a real dread of the cup, and a real human yes, given freely to the Father. On this reading, Christ knows from inside what it costs to say yes when everything in you leans the other way. A human will. Not crushed, not erased, but given.
screen: `ONE WILL: A MIDDLE ROAD.` · `MAXIMUS: NOT FULLY HUMAN WITHOUT IT.` · `TWO WILLS, NOT OPPOSED.` · then, large: `NOT MY WILL, BUT THINE BE DONE.` · then: `A REAL YES, FREELY GIVEN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you want today that you may not get, a result, an apology, an easy afternoon, and name it honestly, the way the garden prayer does. Then see if there's a little room to open your hands around it: not to stop wanting, just to loosen your grip. If you pray, say Jesus's words from the garden, not my will, but thine be done; if you don't, simply breathe out with open hands.
Constantinople III. The sixth ecumenical council, which confessed that Christ has a truly human will as well as a divine one, never opposed. Today's word.
Your line: a human will. Tomorrow, the icons come back to Nicaea. Day seven hundred seventy-four, done.

howItsDone: Catholics pray Thy will be done in the Our Father and meditate on Christ's prayer in Gethsemane in the first Sorrowful Mystery of the rosary, the Agony in the Garden.

chat.says: If Jesus is God, did he really want anything for himself in the garden?
options: Yes: he has a real human will, and in the garden it said a real yes.
Yes, and his human will fought his divine will, and won in the end.
No, the prayer was only an example for us; he never dreaded the cup.
chat.meaning: Constantinople III confessed two wills in Christ, divine and human, not opposed; so not my will, but thine, is a real human yes.

notes: CCC 475 gives the sixth ecumenical council, Constantinople III, in 681: two wills and two natural operations, not opposed, the human will following and submitting to the divine. Paraphrased; the year and 'sixth' rest on it.
Monothelitism described as 'a middle road to bring divided churches back together' without naming it; confirm framing.

Maximus the Confessor's argument and 'what Christ did not take on, he did not heal' (a patristic axiom usually traced to Gregory of Nazianzus) now attributed to 'the Fathers' generally; confirm. 'Tradition says he paid dearly' alludes to his mutilation and exile; confirm.
Gethsemane 'across the valley from Jerusalem' (Mount of Olives): Luke 22:39 says the Mount of Olives; confirm phrasing.
howItsDone: Agony in the Garden as first Sorrowful Mystery; confirm.
